extraction.name: COMMONSENSE QA
extraction.description: A challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering containing 12,247 multiple-choice questions generated from ConceptNet via crowd workers.
extraction.creator: Alon Talmor; Jonathan Herzig; Nicholas Lourie; Jonathan Berant
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were generated by extracting subgraphs from ConceptNet, asking crowd workers to author three multiple-choice questions per subgraph, add two distractors, verify question quality, and then adding Google search snippets as textual context.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: ConceptNet triplets and Google search result snippets.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: ConceptNet triplets were filtered by relation type, English language, concept length, and edit distance before forming question sets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers authored three questions per question set, added two distractors per question, and a disjoint group of workers verified each question by marking it unanswerable or selecting the correct answer.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Each question was verified by two workers, and only questions verified by at least one worker who answered correctly were kept; this filtered out 15% of questions.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Questions often require background knowledge that is seldom explicitly reported on the web due to reporting bias; the paper also discusses the challenge of annotation artifacts and distributional biases in commonsense datasets.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset remains much easier for humans than current models, and retrieved web snippets do not appear to provide much useful information.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluating commonsense question answering and natural language understanding models; the dataset is split into training, development, and test sets.

name.evidence: To investigate question answering with prior knowledge, we present COMMONSENSE QA: a challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering.

description.evidence: To investigate question answering with prior knowledge, we present COMMONSENSE QA: a challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering. We create 12,247 questions through this procedure.

url.evidence: The dataset can be downloaded from www. tau-nlp.org/commonsenseqa .

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We generate multiple-choice questions in a process that comprises the following steps. 1. We extract subgraphs from CONCEPTNET, each with one source concept and three target concepts. 2. We ask crowdsourcing workers to author three questions per subgraph (one per target concept), to add two additional distractors per question, and to verify questions’ quality. 3. We add textual context to each question by querying a search engine and retrieving web snippets.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: We extract subgraphs from CONCEPTNET, each with one source concept and three target concepts. We ask crowdsourcing workers to author three questions per subgraph (one per target concept), to add two additional distractors per question, and to verify questions’ quality. We issue a web query to Google search for every question and candidate answer, concatenating the answer to the question.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: CONCEPTNET is a graph knowledge-base G(C×R×C), where the nodes C represent natural language concepts, and edges R represent commonsense relations. We take the first 100 result snippets for each of the five answer candidates, yielding a context of 500 snippets per question.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: To select a subset of triplets for crowdsourcing we take the following steps: 1. We filter triplets with general relations (e.g., RelatedTo) or relations that are already well-explored in NLP (e.g., IsA). In total we use 22 relations. 2. We filter triplets where one of the concepts is more than four words or not in English. 3. We filter triplets where the edit distance between c1 and c2 is too low.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: We used Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers to generate and validate commonsense questions. AMT workers saw, for every question set, the question concept and three answer concepts. They were asked to formulate three questions, where all questions contain the question concept. To make the task more difficult, we ask crowd-workers to add two additional incorrect answers to each formulated question. Verifiers annotate a question as unanswerable, or choose the right answer.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: We used Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers to generate and validate commonsense questions.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Each question is verified by 2 workers, and only questions verified by at least one worker that answered correctly are used. This processes filters out 15% of the questions.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: Each question is verified by 2 workers

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Because questions are generated freely by workers, they often require background knowledge that is trivial to humans but is seldom explicitly reported on the web due to reporting bias (Gordon and Van Durme, 2013). Investigations of commonsense datasets, and of natural language datasets more generally, have revealed the difficulty in creating benchmarks that measure the understanding of a program rather than its ability to take advantage of distributional biases, and to model the annotation process.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: This is well below human accuracy, demonstrating that the benchmark is much easier for humans. We observe that using snippets does not lead to high performance, hinting that they do not carry a lot of useful information.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We present COMMONSENSE QA, a new dataset focusing on commonsense question answering. We split the data into a training/development/test set with an 80/10/10 split.
